{"docket_number": "77-1177", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1978", "first_party": "Scott", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Illinois", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "Supreme Court of Illinois", "argued": ["1978-12-04T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Did the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments require Illinois to provide Scott with trial counsel?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Scott was convicted in a bench trial of shoplifting and fined $50. The statute applicable to his case set the maximum penalty at a $500 fine and/or one year in jail.

", "conclusion": "

A plurality held that Illinois had not violated the Constitution. Writing for four of the justices, Rehnquist clarified the Court's holding in Argersinger v. Hamlin (1972) and argued that states could only sentence a convicted criminal to imprisonment if that person had been represented by counsel. Since Scott was not sentenced to imprisonment, even though the applicable statute allowed for it, the state was not obligated to provide counsel. Rehnquist called that line of reasoning "the central premise of Argersinger."

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in Scott against Illinois. Mr. Elson, I think you may proceed now, whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. On January 31, 1972, in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, Petitioner Aubrey Scott was convicted of misdemeanor theft, for which he was fined $50. In Illinois, the maximum penalty authorized for this crime is one-year imprisonment and or a $500 fine. On direct appeal of this conviction, the Illinois appellate and Supreme Courts held that under Illinois law and the United States Constitution, Scott had no right to counsel or appointed counsel at trial since he was fined and not imprisoned. The court, this court, accepted certiorari on two questions. First, whether the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to counsel to a defendant charged with an offense punishable in law by imprisonment, regardless of whether a defendant is imprisoned. And second, whether a petitioner's trial was so unfair as to deny due process. Now, the trial in this case was not quite what Mr. Justice Rehnquist just alluded to, summary hanging for shoplifting, but it wasn't that far either. With the exception of the right to jury trial, Scott was not advised by the trial court of any of the constitutional safeguards that this court has found fundamental to fairness in a criminal trial. Your position would apply equally to a $1 fine, would it not? In this case, it would, yes. That is, so long as the judge was empowered under the statute to impose a sentence of imprisonment. Of up to one year. Well, so long as, I understand your position would be the same, to answer the question of the Chief Justice, if punishment actually imposed were a $1 fine, so long as the statute creating the criminal offense had authorized the trial judge to impose a sentence of confinement, even of one day. Well, we don't necessarily go that far in our brief, and the facts of this case don't require that. Supposedly, the court, if it should deem it appropriate, could make a six-month rule, as it did in the jury trial case. Well, what if the particular provision, the penalty provision, was a fine of not exceeding $100, nothing else, no imprisonment at all, then would your position be the same as you're asserting in your briefs and here today? Well, our case certainly wouldn't be the same, but our position would be that the crime of misdemeanor theft is sufficiently established at common law and in the minds of the community as a criminal offense that it would invoke the Sixth Amendment safeguards. Now, the court could make a six-month rule, as you said, but in Argersinger it didn't. Yes. So you're asking us to wholly review Argersinger, everything about it. Is that it? No. Argersinger, of course, explicitly refused to decide the question in this case. But it did hold that if there's to be a sentence of confinement, there has to have been counsel at the criminal trial. And you abandon that argument now. Certainly we abandon, we oppose that. You wholly disregard Argersinger in every respect, that's what it comes down to, isn't it? Well, not the rationale of Argersinger, but we certainly oppose a ruling that you're not entitled to counsel. If a penalty is a prison, it's not a prison. You said that everything is especially just the offense of deciding this case. I'm not sure I agree with you. I mean, presumptively, all state action, including this one, is constitutional unless it's found to violate the federal constitution. And the fact that Argersinger didn't expressly say this state action is all right doesn't mean it's an open question. Well, except that the opinion expressly stated that I think was Mr. Justice Powell and his concurring opinion raised the question, well, what about cases where the prison man is authorized and no jail is imposed? And Mr. Justice Douglas explicitly stated we're not deciding that. And I think that's in line with the tradition in Powell v. Alabama and Gideon v. Wainwright. But did we need to decide it? Was there any occasion to decide it? No. My understanding is, frankly, that the petitioners in that case actually did not ask for such a broad rule. They just said imprisonment only. So it really wasn't put before the court. That's my understanding. And I'd just like to briefly refer to the facts because I think they do make a telling point as to the importance of right to counsel. So, Scott, in this case, was not advised of and did not exercise the right to cross-examination, the right to compulsory process of witnesses, the right to make a closing summation, the right to be informed of the elements of the charge against him, and, of course, the right to counsel, either at his own expense or at the state expense if he could not afford counsel. Now, he was allowed to tell his side of the story, but he was not told that he did not have to tell his side of the story. The trial itself was a paradigm of the prejudice that results when a defendant is without counsel in a criminal trial. The clearest example of this prejudice is that a directed verdict motion should have been made and granted after the state had rested because the state had failed to prove a necessary element of its shoplifting prosecution that Scott, in fact, had not paid for the item he allegedly stole. And Scott, as a layman, had no reason to know that a directed verdict motion could even be made. And I think further prejudice is evident from the fact that after both the state and Scott had rested, the judge admitted that he still had several doubts about the case. What if the state, instead of having this in the criminal system, had called it a civil fine situation and put a maximum of a $500 civil fine, said we're just going to take shoplifting out of the criminal area, and the judge had imposed precisely the same fine at the close of this hearing under a system like that? Would you say he was entitled to counsel? Well, of course, that would be a closer case, but I still think that the crime of theft is so associated in our history and in the popular mind with the criminal element of criminal prosecution that I think counsel probably would be required. So a suggestion in one of the briefs, I don't remember whether it's yours or not, that states can deal with this problem by simply taking certain offenses out of the criminal system entirely wouldn't apply in your case? I don't believe so. I think it would apply, say, jaywalking, that type of thing. You keep talking about robbery. Just shoplifting, huh? Well, it's defined as theft under Illinois law. It's theft under $150. It was shoplifting in this case. But you keep saying how horrible a crime it is. I mean, I don't think any adjectives are going to help this case. Except that Illinois classifies it as theft, and they deem it sufficiently serious to authorize a year's imprisonment. But you indicated your argument would be the same, even if it provided for no imprisonment but only a fine. I think the balance in that case, it would still be criminal. But again, I think... The answer to my question, yes or no? That I, in that case, I think you'd be entitled to the right to counsel. But I respectfully urge that. It's certainly not our case. Would you be entitled to the right to counsel going to spitting on the sidewalk for a minute? Well, if the state authorized year's imprisonment, I think that's the prime determinant of what is a criminal offense, and yes. So it's the... If you had a... The consul would probably be appropriate in that case. And the difference is... The difference is that in that case, it would not have the element... Of the indicia of what is a criminal offense within the meaning of the Sixth Amendment. Which is... Which are... Well, the court has identified seven or eight factors in various cases to define what... Well, which one are you relying on? ...is criminal. We rely really on all of them, because with misdemeanor theft, they all come together to show this is criminal. They... This has a year's imprisonment. It has the requirement of see-enter. It was considered malum in se. It was indictable at common law. This court in Middendorf said larceny, which is basically the same thing, carries the stamp of bad character. It has every criteria. Larceny is the same as robbery? As shoplifting? As shoplifting? Well, it shows the intent to steal, I think. Larceny. I'm sorry, I said larceny. Oh, I'm sorry. Oh, I'm sorry. Larceny. Just so that I have your position in mind, of course, arsony, argon slinger, I'll never know how to pronounce that case, told if there's in fact imprisonment, there must be counsel. We don't have that case. You, as I understand, you make alternative arguments. One, that if the statute authorized imprisonment for up to a year or more, then the crime would be sufficiently serious, there ought to be counsel. Or alternatively, I understand you to say, that even if the statute does not authorize imprisonment, but the statute has all the other indicia of a common law crime, then that should be right to counsel. But that case isn't before it. Right. I don't think I have to make that case for this. It's only the first one we're dealing with today, is when the statute in fact authorizes a year imprisonment, and it is also a traditional common law crime, is there a right to counsel there? That's what we're dealing with. That's correct. That's the only issue I see in this case. Your theory is such that, in conjunction with the question by Mr. Justice Stewart a moment ago, your theory is that this is just kind of an unrolling thing, and it's unrolled from Powell to Gideon to Argersinger, and these are just way stations, and presumably this is another way station, and a year from now we'll be asked to expand it further. Well, the Sixth Amendment right to counsel has been termed an evolving concept. Do you think that's the way the framers intended? It's hard to say. Do you really think it's hard to say? What the framers intended? Well, there are certain things about the Sixth Amendment right to counsel's application now that clearly had no idea. My question is, do you think it's difficult to say what the framers of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel thought about it? Oh, not in this case. No, I didn't mean in this case. I meant generally. Oh, yes, of course. You think it is difficult? Well, yes. But isn't it really quite clear that, as far as the framers' intent went, it wouldn't have applied at all to a state trial. All it did was guarantee in the Sixth Amendment, that it decided in a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and a 10-year-old general, and he wanted to bring a lawyer along at his own expense to assist him. That's what it meant. Every historian knows that. Every schoolboy said that. Right. Is that correct? I believe so. We've come a long way from there, haven't we? Yes, indeed. And I think the framers, it is clear that the framers intended that the right to counsel was essential in all criminal prosecutions at that time. Well, but the right to counsel is defined by my brother Stewart. If you could afford a lawyer and pay for him and bring him along, and you were being tried in the federal court, you could do it. Yes, that's right. Now, your position, I want to be sure I understand it, is that shoplifting from a store, for all purposes of the stigma and consequences, shoplifting from a store is no different from shoplifting from a bank. In Illinois, if it were charged as theft under $150, it is no different. That's correct. His record says theft. Of the five grounds for reversal set forth in Petitioner's Brief, Petitioner relies most strongly, as I indicated, on the Sixth Amendment ground. And there are two alternative rationales for applying the Sixth Amendment right to counsel in this case. The first and simplest is that the right to counsel applies as the terms of the Sixth Amendment specified in all criminal prosecutions. And the court has never limited the application of any Sixth Amendment right that has been applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment on the basis of the gravity of the crime, except, of course, for the right to jury trial. But in Argersinger, the court pointed out that the historical reasons for limiting the right to jury to serious offenses do not exist with respect to the right to counsel. And the court specifically rejected the premise that crimes punishable by less than six months' imprisonment may be tried without a lawyer simply because they may be tried without a jury. And the right to counsel also requires wider application than the right to jury because of the nature of the criminal trial process. And the court has repeatedly pointed out that the right to counsel and not the right to jury is essential to a fair trial to the integrity of the fact-finding process. And as the court pointed out in Fuller v. Oregon, the right to counsel is necessary so that defendants may recognize and take advantage of the Sixth Amendment's other fair trial safeguards. Since the right to counsel is therefore the Sixth Amendment right that is most important to the actual achievement of a fair trial, it would contradict the Sixth Amendment's essential purpose of assuring fair trials to apply the right to counsel more narrowly than the other Sixth Amendment rights. Moreover, respondent's argument that the right to counsel does not apply to petitioner's prosecution renders petitioner's right to a jury trial meaningless. For notwithstanding respondent's assertions to the contrary, a layman simply cannot adequately present a case to a jury in any case. The right to counsel has been much of a man in a time of penicillin law by over six months in prison location. Otherwise, the right to jury would simply be a nullity. The... Yes, I don't happen to agree with your assertion that a layman can't possibly present a defense to a jury if he wants to. If it's a justice of the peace misdemeanor type of jury. In my own practice, I have seen that done. I've never seen it done. It's hard for me as a trial lawyer to envision it. I have... Have you never seen jury... Have you never seen juries acquit defendants who have not chosen to retain counsel on relatively low-grade misdemeanors? I have never seen it. There aren't that many misdemeanor jury trials in the area where I practice. Now, if the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is to be applied according to its terms in all criminal prosecutions, then there is only one issue in this case, and that is whether a prosecution for misdemeanor theft not resulting in imprisonment is a criminal prosecution within the meaning of the Sixth Amendment. And as I previously stated, in this case, it has all the indicia of what is a criminal prosecution, and I don't think respondents really contest that this is not, in fact, a criminal prosecution. But regardless of whether the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is to be applied according to its terms, the right applies in this case under the test used for applying any Sixth Amendment right to the states, and that is whether or not it is necessary for fundamental fairness. Now, counsel is as fundamental to fairness in the trial of a misdemeanor that does not result in imprisonment as it was in Gideon in the trial of a felony and as it was in Argersinger in the trial of a misdemeanor resulting in imprisonment. There is no functional difference between the trial of a felony and a misdemeanor that would make a layman a more competent advocate in one than in the other. If an unconstitutional misdemeanor trial and conviction of a felony imprisonment does not comport with fundamental fairness as Argersinger held, then fundamental fairness also must be denied by an unconstitutional misdemeanor trial and conviction that does not result in imprisonment because a trial cannot simply be suddenly transformed into a fair fact-finding process because after the trial the judge decides not to sentence the defendant to jail.
